summary: Extends IS-IS to support optimal routing in a domain with two levels. It changes how routes are passed down from one level to the other so that a router can choose the best path, instead of being limited by route summarization between levels. It replaces RFC 2966 and extends the semantics of RFC 1195.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS networks are split into areas, and a level 2 backbone connects them. This document lets detailed prefixes travel between the levels, so that routers compute better paths, and adds one bit that marks a route as having come from above so it is never sent back up and does not loop.

questions: what is the is-is up down bit
is-is level 1 to level 2 route leaking
subtitle: How IS-IS routers in a two-level network can share detailed prefixes between levels without creating routing loops.

tldr.problem: In a two-level IS-IS domain, routers only exchange summaries of each area's prefixes, so a router outside an area cannot compute a good path into it, and cannot pick the best exit point.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the IS-IS semantics so that level 2 routes can be advertised into level 1, and marks them with an up/down bit so that a router never advertises them back up the hierarchy, which is what would create a forwarding loop.
tldr.outcome: Routes computed inside the domain become more accurate, at the cost of more prefixes to carry. The document replaces RFC 2966 and updates RFC 1195.

facts.label: Up/down bit
facts.value: Bit 8 of the default metric field in TLVs 128 and 130

today: RFC 5302 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It replaces RFC 2966, which was Informational, and has not been obsoleted since. It updates RFC 1195 with the up/down bit and the rules for advertising level 2 routes into level 1.

sections.title: Two-Level IS-IS and Its Limits
sections.content:
The document describes extensions to the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol to support optimal routing within a two-level domain. IS-IS itself is specified in ISO 10589, with extensions for supporting IPv4 given in RFC 1195. The document replaces RFC 2966, which was an Informational document, and no other intentional substantive changes were made to it.

An IS-IS routing domain, an autonomous system running IS-IS, can be partitioned into multiple level 1 areas and a level 2 connected subset of the topology that interconnects all of the level 1 areas. Within each level 1 area, all routers exchange link state information, and level 2 routers also exchange level 2 link state information to compute routes between areas.

RFC 1195 defines the Type, Length and Value tuples used to carry IPv4 routing information in IS-IS, and the semantics and procedures for interactions between levels. Routers in a level 1 area exchange information within that area, and for IP destinations not found among the prefixes in the level 1 database, the level 1 router should forward packets to the nearest router that is in both level 1 and level 2, an L1L2 router, with the 'attached bit' set in its level 1 Link State Protocol Data Unit. Also per RFC 1195, an L1L2 router should be manually configured with a set of prefixes summarising the IP prefixes reachable in that level 1 area, and these summaries are injected into level 2. RFC 1195 specifies no further interactions between level 1 and level 2 for IPv4 prefixes, and this document extends those semantics so that a domain running both level 1 and level 2 routers can distribute IP prefixes between the levels and back, with restrictions that keep persistent forwarding loops from forming. The goal is to increase the granularity of the routing information within the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Today a router outside an area only knows a summary of that area's addresses, so it has to guess which way in is best. This document lets the real prefixes cross the levels, and adds the rule that keeps that from causing loops.

sections.title: Why Share More Prefixes, and What It Costs
sections.content:
The mechanisms in RFC 1195 lead to excellent scalability properties, but in certain circumstances the administrator may wish to sacrifice some scalability and distribute more specific information than RFC 1195 describes.

The first reason is the quality of the resulting routes. A well-known property of prefix summarization is that it necessarily results in a loss of information, which in turn results in the computation of a route based on less information, and that will frequently produce routes that are not optimal. The RFC's example: suppose a level 1 area has two L1L2 routers that both advertise a single summary of all prefixes in the area. Any other level 2 router computes the shortest path to one of the two L1L2 routers, and if they are equidistant it picks one arbitrarily. That router may not be the optimal one when viewed from the level 1 topology, and the path from it to the destination may even traverse the L1L2 router that was not selected. More detailed topological or metric information would let the level 2 router compute a more optimal route. The situation is symmetric: a level 1 router has no information about prefixes in level 2 or in another level 1 area, and using the nearest L1L2 router is effectively injecting a default route without metric information into the level 1 area.

The second driver is shortest exit routing. When a router learns multiple possible paths to external destinations via BGP, it selects only one of those routes for the forwarding table, and one factor in the BGP route selection is the IGP cost to the BGP next hop address. Many ISP networks depend on this technique. If a level 1 router does not know the exact IGP metric to all BGP speakers in other level 1 areas, it cannot do effective shortest exit routing.

The third driver is the use of the IGP metric as part of the BGP Multi-Exit Discriminator. Current practice is to take the IS-IS metric and insert it as the MED value, which tends to cause external traffic to enter the domain at the point closest to the exit router. That works in single-area networks but becomes problematic once hierarchy is installed, because the loss of end-to-end metric information means the MED value will not reflect the true distance across the advertising domain. Full distribution of prefix information within the domain would allow an accurate computation of the IS-IS metric across the domain, and therefore an accurate MED value.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things improve when the real prefixes are known: the path a router picks, the exit point it chooses for outside traffic, and the metric it advertises to other networks. The cost is that the domain now carries more prefixes.

sections.title: The Scalability Trade-Off
sections.content:
The disadvantage of domain-wide prefix distribution is its impact on the scalability of IS-IS. Areas help scalability because LSPs are contained within a single area, which limits the size of the link state database, and that in turn limits the complexity of the shortest path computation. Summarizing prefix information helps too, because the abstraction removes the sheer number of data items to be transported and the number of routes to be computed.

The RFC notes that distributing prefixes on a domain-wide basis impacts the second of those aspects only. It will increase the number of prefixes throughout the domain, which results in increased memory consumption, transmission requirements and computation requirements throughout the domain. It has no effect whatsoever on the first aspect, namely the existence of areas and the limitation of the distribution of the link state database.

The net result is that introducing domain-wide prefix distribution into a formerly flat, single-area network is a clear benefit to the scalability of that network, but it is a compromise and does not provide the maximum scalability available with IS-IS. Domains that use the facility should be aware of the trade-off between scalability and optimality, and provision and monitor their networks accordingly; normal provisioning guidelines for a fully hierarchical deployment of IS-IS do not apply to this configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Distributing more prefixes makes the link state database bigger and the path computation heavier. It does not change how the domain is split into areas. The RFC calls the result a compromise, not a free win.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit and Level 2 Routes in Level 1
sections.content:
The document defines how level 2 routes are advertised in level 1 LSPs, as an extension of the encoding in RFC 1195. To some extent the level 2 backbone can be seen as a separate area itself. RFC 1195 allows L1L2 routers to advertise IP routes learned via level 1 routing into level 2, and those inter-area routes must be advertised in level 2 LSPs in the 'IP Internal Reachability Information' TLV, TLV 128. Intra-area level 2 routes are advertised in the same TLV, so level 1 to level 2 inter-area routes are indistinguishable from level 2 intra-area routes.

RFC 1195 does not define level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes. A simple extension would allow an L1L2 router to advertise routes learned via level 2 routing in its level 1 LSP, but to prevent routing loops, L1L2 routers MUST NOT advertise level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes that they learn via level 1 routing back into level 2. There must therefore be a way to distinguish level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes from level 1 intra-area routes. RFC 5305 defines an 'up/down bit' for this purpose in the extended IP reachability TLV, TLV 135.

This document takes a different route. TLVs 128 and 130 have a Metric field consisting of four Type of Service metrics, and the first metric, the 'default metric', has its high-order bit reserved as bit 8, which routers must set to zero on transmission and ignore on receipt. The document redefines that high-order bit in the default metric field of TLVs 128 and 130 to be the up/down bit. L1L2 routers MUST set it to one for prefixes derived from level 2 routing and advertised into level 1 LSPs, and it MUST be set to zero for all other IP prefixes in level 1 or level 2 LSPs. Prefixes with the up/down bit set that are learned via level 1 routing MUST NOT be advertised by L1L2 routers back into level 2.

The document also clarifies the route-type and metric-type rules. TLV 128 is 'IP Internal Reachability Information' and should carry prefixes directly connected to IS-IS routers, while TLV 130 is 'IP External Reachability Information' and should carry routes learned from outside the IS-IS domain. Metrics of the internal metric-type should be used when the metric is comparable to metrics used to weigh links inside the domain, and metrics of the external metric-type when it cannot be directly compared; the external metric-type can only be used for external IP prefixes, so it should never be seen in TLV 128. Routers MUST give the same preference to IP routes advertised in the internal and external TLVs when they carry an internal metric, and IP routes advertised in the external TLV with the external metric-type MUST be given less preference than the same routes advertised with the internal metric-type, regardless of the metric values.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing IS-IS prefix TLVs had one reserved bit that every router was told to ignore. This document gives that bit a meaning: it marks a prefix that came from level 2, so that it can be sent down to level 1 but never back up.

sections.title: The Types of IP Routes in IS-IS
sections.content:
RFC 1195 and this document define several ways of advertising IP routes, with four variables involved: the level of the LSP in which the route is advertised, level 1 or level 2; the route-type, derived from the type of TLV, with internal routes in TLV 128 and external routes in TLV 130; the metric-type, internal or external, derived from the internal/external metric-type bit in the Metric field, bit 7; and whether the route is leaked down the hierarchy and so cannot be advertised back up, which is derived from the newly defined up/down bit in the default Metric field.

The combination of internal reachability information with an external metric-type is not allowed, and the up/down bit MUST NOT be set in level 2 LSPs. That leaves eight types of IP advertisement in IS-IS. Level 1 intra-area routes are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 128 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, and the prefixes are directly connected to the advertising router. Level 1 external routes are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, and the prefixes are learned from other IGPs.

Level 2 intra-area routes are advertised in level 2 LSPs in TLV 128 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, and cannot be distinguished from level 1 to level 2 inter-area routes. Level 2 external routes are advertised in level 2 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, and cannot be distinguished from level 1 to level 2 inter-area external routes. Level 1 to level 2 inter-area routes are advertised in level 2 LSPs in TLV 128 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, derived during the level 1 SPF computation from prefixes advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 128. Their external counterparts are advertised in level 2 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit zero and an internal metric, derived from level 1 LSPs in TLV 130.

Level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 128 with the up/down bit set to one and an internal metric, learned via level 2 routing and derived during the level 2 SPF computation. Their external counterparts are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit set to one and an internal metric. Level 1 external routes with an external metric are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit zero, as are level 2 external routes with an external metric in level 2 LSPs, which cannot be distinguished from level 1 to level 2 inter-area external routes with an external metric. Level 2 to level 1 inter-area external routes with an external metric are advertised in level 1 LSPs in TLV 130 with the up/down bit set to one.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the level, the TLV type, the metric type and the new bit gives eight distinct kinds of prefix advertisement, and the RFC lists each one with the TLV it travels in and the bits it carries.

sections.title: Order of Preference
sections.content:
IS-IS cannot depend on metrics alone for route selection. Some types of route must always be preferred over others, regardless of the costs computed in the Dijkstra calculation. One reason is that inter-area routes can only be advertised with a maximum metric of 63, and that value of 63 does not mean infinity, as a hop count of 16 does in RIP. Introducing an infinity cost for IS-IS inter-area routes would introduce counting-to-infinity behaviour through two or more L1L2 routers, which would have a bad impact on network stability.

The order of preference rests on four assumptions from RFC 1195: routes derived from level 1 routing are preferred over routes derived from level 2 routing; internal routes with internal metric-type and external prefixes with internal metric-type have the same preference; external routes with internal metric-type are preferred over external routes with external metric-type; and routes derived from level 2 routing are preferred over level 2 to level 1 routes derived from level 1 routing.

From those the document derives six levels of preference. First come level 1 intra-area routes with an internal metric and level 1 external routes with an internal metric. Second come level 2 intra-area routes with an internal metric, level 2 external routes with an internal metric, level 1 to level 2 inter-area routes with an internal metric, and level 1 to level 2 inter-area external routes with an internal metric. Third come level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes with an internal metric, and level 2 to level 1 inter-area external routes with an internal metric. Fourth come level 1 external routes with an external metric. Fifth come level 2 external routes with an external metric, and level 1 to level 2 inter-area external routes with an external metric. Sixth come level 2 to level 1 inter-area external routes with an external metric.
sections.plainLanguage: When two routes compete, IS-IS does not simply take the lower metric. It has a fixed ranking of route kinds, and the ranking puts local area routes first and routes that came down from level 2 last.

sections.title: Compatibility With Older Routers
sections.content:
The solution in the document is not fully compatible with RFC 1195; it is an extension to it. If routers do not use the new functionality of external level 1 routes or level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes, older implementations that strictly follow RFC 1195 will be compatible with newer implementations that follow this document.

Implementations that do not accept the 'IP External Reachability Information' TLV in level 1 LSPs will not be able to compute external level 1 routes. That could cause routing loops between level 1-only routers that do understand external level 1 routes for a particular destination and level 1-only routers that use the default route pointing to the closest attached L1L2 router for that destination. Implementations that follow RFC 1195 SHOULD ignore bit 8 in the default Metric field when computing routes, so even older implementations that do not know of the up/down bit should be able to accept the new level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes; they will install them as level 1 intra-area routes, which does not by itself cause routing loops among level 1-only routers.

It is vital, however, that the up/down bit is recognised by L1L2 routers. Older implementations that follow RFC 1195 and do not understand the bit will treat the level 2 to level 1 inter-area routes as level 1 intra-area routes, and will advertise these routes back into level 2, which can cause routing loops, sub-optimal routing or extra routing instability. For this reason, it is RECOMMENDED that implementations by default do not advertise any level 2 routes into level 1, and that implementations SHOULD force the network administrator to configure L1L2 routers manually to advertise any level 2 routes into level 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers ignore the new bit, which is harmless among level 1 routers. It is the routers that sit between the levels that must understand it, because an old one would send a level 2 route back up and cause a loop. The RFC therefore says the feature should be off until an administrator turns it on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document raises no new security issues for IS-IS. For the general security considerations for IS-IS, the RFC points at RFC 5304, which covers IS-IS cryptographic authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes the security of IS-IS. The authentication rules are in a separate document.

viz.caption: Three reasons to distribute prefixes across the levels

items.title: Better routes
items.text: Summaries lose information, so a router outside an area cannot see which way in is actually best.

items.title: Shortest exit routing
items.text: Choosing which BGP route to install depends on the IGP cost to the next hop, which a level 1 router cannot know without the real prefixes.

items.title: A meaningful MED
items.text: The metric advertised to other domains is the IS-IS metric, which is wrong if the end-to-end metric is not known inside the domain.
